params.text:
Welcome to This Module

Artificial intelligence is no longer a future prospect — it is actively reshaping research methodologies across every academic and scientific domain. With that transformation comes a pressing challenge: how do Research Ethics Committees (RECs) and researchers ensure that AI-assisted projects remain safe, fair, and legally compliant?

This module — Responsible Oversight in AI-Enabled Research — is designed to give you the practical frameworks, evaluation principles, and regulatory knowledge required to rigorously assess AI-related research proposals.

Learning Goals

  1. Explain the AI Lifecycle Approach and identify the REC's scope within it.
  2. Apply the five foundational evaluation questions to any AI research proposal.
  3. Analyse the ten core ethical principles specific to machine learning systems.
  4. Interpret the EU AI Act's risk-based classification and FRIA requirements.
  5. Select the appropriate ethics self-assessment tool for a given research context.
  6. Evaluate real-world AI proposals using structured REC review checklists.

Estimated duration: 60–75 minutes  |  Chapters: 19  |  Interactive questions: 26

params.text:
Ethics Across Every Phase

Traditional research ethics oversight operated as a one-time pre-approval gate: a committee reviewed a fixed proposal and granted clearance. Machine learning changes that logic. Because these algorithms adapt to new data during deployment, a single point-in-time oversight is no longer sufficient. Ethical responsibility must map directly to the software development lifecycle.

The AI Lifecycle Approach identifies four phases where ethics must be actively integrated:

  • Design — goal-setting, data strategy, system architecture
  • Development — model training, testing, bias auditing
  • Deployment — release, integration into live environments
  • Use & Monitoring — ongoing performance review, redress, retraining

panels.title: What does the REC evaluate?

params.text:
The REC's scope focuses entirely on mitigating ethical risks stemming from the research methodology. Evaluation covers four structural boundaries:

  • Protection — methods to protect participant privacy and anonymize data
  • Safety — whether research poses a serious risk to the interests and safety of subjects
  • Consent — ensuring informed, valid consent is obtained
  • Compliance — adherence to local data protection and IP ownership laws

panels.title: Why is lifecycle thinking important for AI?

params.text: Unlike static software, machine learning models evolve. A model trained on historical data may drift in performance as real-world data patterns change. Ethical commitments made at the design phase — such as fairness guarantees or consent boundaries — must be re-evaluated at every subsequent phase, not treated as fixed one-time obligations.

panels.title: What phase follows Deployment?

params.text: Use & Monitoring. Once an AI system is live, continuous oversight is essential to manage real-world performance, detect unexpected harms, and ensure the system continues to meet its original ethical commitments. This phase also includes providing redress mechanisms for affected parties.

params.title: Test your recall

dialogs.answer: A framework requiring ethical considerations to be actively integrated across all four phases of AI development: Design, Development, Deployment, and Use & Monitoring.
Focuses on mitigating ethical risks from research methodology, covering Protection, Safety, Consent, and Compliance.
Bridging the Gap in Research Ethics Training and Education — an Erasmus+ project equipping REC members and researchers with AI ethics knowledge.

params.text:
The Turing Way Framework: Five Pillars

Before applying any specialised AI ethics tool, every proposal must address five foundational questions. Derived from The Turing Way template, these pillars establish the baseline information required for any assessment. Without these specific inputs, there is no evidentiary basis for certifying that a prototype meets institutional or legal standards.

panels.title: 1. Project Description — What is the ultimate goal?

params.text: The researcher must describe the project's purpose, core research question, and intended real-world application with precision. Vague descriptions of intent are insufficient for ethical clearance.

panels.title: 2. Data & Methodology — What data, why, and how?

params.text: The researcher must explain exactly what data will be collected or used, why it is necessary (data minimisation), and precisely how it will be processed. This includes identifying whether data is primary or secondary, and whether it contains sensitive personal information.

panels.title: 3. Consent — How is freely-given informed consent ensured?

params.text: Participants must provide consent that is freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. For AI systems using secondary data, the committee must verify that the original consent covered the proposed new use.

panels.title: 4. Privacy & Security — How is sensitive information protected?

params.text: The proposal must specify how sensitive information is technically secured and restricted to pertinent team members only. This covers both organisational access controls and technical protection measures such as encryption and pseudonymisation.

panels.title: 5. Further Societal Consequences — What are the positive and negative impacts?

params.text: The researcher must describe both the intended societal benefits and the potential negative consequences of the work. This includes broader impacts on communities, not just direct research participants.

params.title: Test your recall

dialogs.answer: Describe the project's ultimate goal and core purpose — what problem is being solved and for whom.
Explain what specific data will be used, why it is necessary, and exactly how it will be utilised.
How will you ensure any personal data collected is done so with freely-given, informed consent?
How will you ensure sensitive information is kept secure and accessible only to pertinent team members?
Describe both the positive and negative potential societal impacts of your work.
Using data for a purpose other than the one for which it was originally collected — requires explicit re-consent or legal basis.

params.text:
Control & Privacy: The First Category

The first category of core AI ethical issues addresses the fundamental questions of who controls AI decisions and how personal data is protected. These two principles are closely intertwined: meaningful human oversight is impossible without knowing how data flows through the system, and robust data governance is meaningless if humans cannot intervene when the system fails.

panels.title: Human Agency and Oversight

params.text:
Core Principle: Researchers must ensure absolute human control over AI decisions to prevent automated systems from overriding human judgement.

REC Focus Questions:

  • Who makes the final decision — the AI system or a human professional?
  • Is meaningful, actionable human oversight retained throughout the entire process?
  • Can a human override or validate the AI's output at any point?

panels.title: Privacy and Data Governance

params.text:
Core Principle: AI systems inherently rely on massive datasets that frequently encompass highly sensitive personal data. The ethical use and technical protection of this data is a core research obligation.

REC Focus Questions:

  • Is participant consent valid for the specific data use proposed?
  • How is the data technically protected against unauthorised access?
  • Is there any risk of secondary use — repurposing data for a different aim than originally consented to?

params.title: Test your recall

dialogs.answer: The principle requiring researchers to ensure human control over AI decisions, so automated systems cannot override human judgement.
Addressing the ethical use of large, sensitive datasets and ensuring their technical protection through encryption, access controls, and data minimisation.
The risk that data collected for one purpose will be repurposed for another without adequate consent — a key concern for REC review.
The tendency of human professionals to over-rely on automated outputs, reducing their independent critical evaluation of AI-generated alerts or recommendations.

params.text:
Clarity & Understanding: The Second Category

Transparency and Explainability are distinct but complementary principles. Transparency addresses whether the system's operation is open to scrutiny; Explainability addresses whether the outputs of that system can be understood by the people affected by them. Both are essential for trustworthy AI — and the failure of either can invalidate an otherwise technically sound research proposal.

panels.title: Transparency

params.text:
Core Principle: There must be absolute clarity regarding how data is processed and how algorithmic decisions are made.

REC Focus Questions:

  • Can research participants understand what the AI system does with their data?
  • Is the underlying methodology fully transparent to reviewers and regulators?
  • Is the system a 'black box' — opaque even to its developers?

panels.title: Explainability

params.text:
Core Principle: AI outputs and predictions must be comprehensible and explainable to all relevant stakeholders — not just data scientists, but also clinicians, students, support staff, and the participants themselves.

REC Focus Questions:

  • Is explainability structurally addressed in the methodology?
  • Who is qualified to interpret the results, and how will that interpretation be communicated?
  • If a person is denied access or flagged as 'at risk', can the reason be explained clearly?

panels.title: Transparency vs. Explainability — the key difference

params.text: Transparency is about the system: can we see how it processes data? Explainability is about the output: can a specific prediction or decision be explained to the person it affects? A system can be technically transparent (all code is open-source) yet still produce predictions that no one can explain in plain language.

params.title: Test your recall

dialogs.answer: Ensuring absolute clarity regarding how data is processed and how algorithmic decisions are made — the 'open box' requirement.
Ensuring that AI outputs and predictions are comprehensible and interpretable to all relevant stakeholders, including non-technical participants.
When an AI model (typically a deep neural network) produces predictions that even its developers cannot explain — a fundamental challenge to both transparency and explainability.
Transparency = openness about HOW the system works. Explainability = clarity about WHY a specific output was generated.

params.text:
Equity & Representation: The Third Category

AI systems learn from historical data — and history is not neutral. When training datasets reflect existing social inequalities, algorithms do not simply reproduce those inequalities: they scale and amplify them. A facial recognition system trained predominantly on light-skinned faces will perform substantially worse on darker-skinned individuals. A student dropout predictor trained on historically biased academic records may disproportionately flag students from lower-income backgrounds.

The REC must ensure that concrete, verified measures are in place to detect and mitigate bias before deployment — not just acknowledge it in a risk register.

panels.title: Fairness and Social Inequality

params.text:
Core Principle: AI systems possess the capacity to reproduce, scale, and amplify existing social biases and inequalities at an unprecedented speed and scale.

REC Focus Questions:

  • Are rigorous fairness audits conducted across demographic groups?
  • Who ultimately benefits from the system, and who potentially loses?
  • Does the system perform equally well for all segments of the target population?

panels.title: Bias, Diversity, and Non-discrimination

params.text:
Core Principle: A critical lack of diverse representation in training datasets can actively harm minority and marginalised groups. Representative data is not optional — it is an ethical requirement.

REC Focus Questions:

  • Has dataset diversity been thoroughly considered and documented?
  • Are concrete bias mitigation strategies in place (e.g. re-sampling, re-weighting, adversarial debiasing)?
  • Has the system been tested on subgroups that may be underrepresented in the training data?

panels.title: What is a fairness audit?

params.text: A structured, evidence-based evaluation of an AI system designed to determine whether it performs equitably across protected demographic groups (e.g. age, gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status). A fairness audit should be conducted both before deployment and during ongoing monitoring. The results must be documented and made available to the REC.

params.title: Test your recall

dialogs.answer: The requirement to prevent AI systems from reproducing, scaling, or amplifying existing social biases through algorithmic decision-making.
Ensuring training datasets are representative of diverse groups to prevent direct harm to minority or marginalised populations.
A rigorous evaluation of an AI system to determine who benefits and who potentially loses from its deployment — must cover demographic subgroups.
Ensuring the system performs accurately for all groups by including representative samples from all relevant demographic subgroups in the training data.

params.text:
Broader Ecosystem Impacts: The Fourth Category

Ethical responsibility does not end with research participants. AI systems operate within broader social and ecological ecosystems, and their impact extends well beyond the individuals directly involved in the study. The REC must consider macro-level implications — from the potential for psychological manipulation of populations, to the carbon footprint generated by training large neural networks on GPU clusters.

panels.title: Societal Well-being

params.text:
Core Principle: Research projects utilising AI must strictly align with the broader public interest and societal good. AI must not be used to manipulate behaviour or undermine democratic processes.

REC Focus Questions:

  • What are the macro-level implications for society if this system scales widely?
  • Is there any potential for psychological or behavioural manipulation of the public?
  • Does the system align with the public interest, or could it concentrate power inequitably?

panels.title: Environmental Well-being

params.text:
Core Principle: The training and deployment of complex AI models can consume disproportionately large amounts of energy. This environmental cost must be accounted for in the research design.

REC Focus Questions:

  • Are environmental sustainability and carbon footprint considerations factored into the system's design?
  • Has the research team considered more energy-efficient model architectures?
  • Is the environmental cost proportionate to the research benefit?

params.title: Test your recall

dialogs.answer: Ensuring research projects and AI systems align with the broader public interest — preventing manipulation, surveillance, or misuse that harms democratic society.
Accounting for the disproportionately large energy consumption of training and deploying complex AI models — the carbon footprint must be factored into research design.
The use of AI systems to influence or alter individual or collective behaviour without explicit, informed consent — a macro-level societal concern.

params.text:
Responsibility & The Future: The Fifth Category

As AI systems become more capable and more interconnected with physical technologies, two final dimensions of ethical risk become critical: Accountability (who bears legal and ethical responsibility when AI fails?) and Convergence (what new ethical risks emerge when AI intersects with robotics, IoT, or neurotechnology?).

panels.title: Accountability

params.text:
Core Principle: There must be unequivocally clear lines of responsibility established for when AI systems fail or cause harm. Ambiguity about who is accountable is itself an ethical failure.

REC Focus Questions:

  • Who is ultimately accountable — the developer, deployer, or user?
  • Is there an established, accessible redress mechanism for affected parties?
  • What happens when an automated decision causes harm — who answers for it?

panels.title: AI Convergence with Other Technologies

params.text:
Core Principle: AI frequently intersects with emerging fields such as robotics, IoT, and neurotechnology. It is important to distinguish between Research ON AI (developing new algorithms) and Research WITH AI (applying existing AI to another domain). Each carries different ethical risk profiles.

REC Focus Questions:

  • Does the convergence of multiple technologies amplify existing ethical risks?
  • If AI is connected to physical sensors or actuators, what new harm pathways are created?

panels.title: Research ON AI vs. Research WITH AI

params.text:
Research ON AI: Advancing AI itself — developing new algorithms, architectures, or training methods. The ethical focus is on the algorithm's properties (bias, interpretability, safety).

Research WITH AI: Applying existing AI technologies to another domain — healthcare, IoT, robotics, neurotech. The ethical focus shifts to the domain-specific risks the AI introduces (e.g. patient safety, physical harm, surveillance).

panels.title: What is a redress mechanism?

params.text: An established and accessible process for affected parties to seek compensation, correction, or explanation when an AI system causes harm. Redress mechanisms must be clearly defined before deployment — not designed reactively after harm occurs. The EU AI Act requires high-risk AI deployers to provide such mechanisms.

params.text:
The EU AI Act: Risk-Based Regulation

The EU AI Act is the world's first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence. It uses a risk-based classification system in which the level of regulatory scrutiny is proportional to the risk the AI system poses to safety and fundamental rights. For RECs, understanding this framework is essential: it determines what level of ethical scrutiny is legally required for any given proposal.

panels.title: Unacceptable Risk — Banned Systems

params.text: AI systems in this category are explicitly prohibited because they represent a clear threat to fundamental rights and human dignity. Examples include: social credit scoring by governments, real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces (with limited exceptions), subliminal manipulation techniques, and AI that exploits vulnerabilities of specific groups.

panels.title: High Risk — Strictly Regulated

params.text: AI systems that could have a significant negative impact on safety or fundamental rights. Includes: AI in education (student assessment, dropout prediction), employment (CV screening, performance monitoring), healthcare (medical diagnosis, treatment recommendation), law enforcement, migration, critical infrastructure, and democratic processes. These systems require rigorous conformity assessment, documentation, and ongoing monitoring.

panels.title: Limited Risk — Transparency Obligations

params.text: AI systems with specific transparency requirements. Primarily applies to systems that interact directly with humans — such as chatbots and AI-generated content — which must be identifiable as AI. Users must be informed they are interacting with an automated system.

panels.title: Minimal Risk — Light Monitoring

params.text: The vast majority of AI applications fall into this category: spam filters, content recommendation, AI in video games, etc. These systems face very few obligations. The Act uses a risk-based approach where scrutiny is proportional to risk — minimal-risk systems are not subject to strict regulatory enforcement or mandatory impact assessments.

panels.title: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA)

params.text: The FRIA is a structured pre-deployment assessment required under the EU AI Act for deployers of high-risk AI in sensitive sectors: public sector, education, employment, law enforcement, migration, and essential services. Its goal is to identify and mitigate potential impacts on fundamental rights before deployment. For all other high-risk cases outside these sensitive areas, a FRIA is strongly recommended.

params.text:
The Legal Architecture of AI Research Ethics

Ethical self-assessment tools operate within — and must be aligned with — a binding legal and regulatory architecture. For AI research in the European Union, five foundational documents define what is required, what is recommended, and what is prohibited. The REC must verify that proposals explicitly reference and integrate the relevant frameworks.

panels.title: 1. Foundational AI Regulation: The AI Act

params.text: The EU AI Act (2024) is the comprehensive European regulatory framework for AI. It establishes risk categories, conformity assessment requirements, technical standards, and enforcement mechanisms. All AI research involving EU participants or deployed within the EU must comply with its requirements.

panels.title: 2. Trustworthy AI & Data Protection: ALTAI + GDPR

params.text:
ALTAI (Assessment List for Trustworthy AI) is based on the EU Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI. It provides the operational checklist for implementing the HLEG's seven key requirements.

GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) is the foundational European law governing data protection and privacy. It applies to all processing of personal data from EU residents, regardless of where the researcher is located.

panels.title: 3. Design & Operational Ethics: Ethics by Design & General-Purpose AI Code of Practice

params.text:
Ethics by Design and Ethics of Use are guiding principles for maintaining ethical integrity throughout the AI lifecycle — from initial design through operational deployment.

The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice provides operational standards for versatile AI models (such as large language models) that can be adapted to multiple uses and therefore present unique governance challenges.

panels.title: REC focus question for legal frameworks

params.text: The committee must ask: Are these specific principles, frameworks, and legal standards explicitly referenced and integrated into the research proposal? A proposal that acknowledges GDPR compliance but ignores the AI Act's risk classification for its context is incomplete and should be returned for revision.

params.text:
The Proposal: Predicting Student Dropout Risk

A university research team proposes developing an AI-based tool to predict the risk of students dropping out before they actually do. The system aims to proactively offer targeted support to at-risk students.

Data sources: Institutional academic records, class attendance, LMS activity logs, socioeconomic background data, and anonymised mental health service usage.

The model: A neural network trained on 5 years of historical student data.

Deployment: Trial phase across two university faculties. Support staff will receive automated alerts about students flagged as "at-risk".

Ethics mitigation provided by the team: The proposal states GDPR compliance and notes that all data is pseudonymised before processing.

params.alt: Exercise: What Would You Ask the PI? 6 Critical Evaluation Parameters for Smart Success — Human Oversight, Bias & Fairness, Explainability, Privacy & Governance, Accountability, Societal Impact

params.text:
The REC Review: Six Critical Questions

Basic legal compliance — GDPR adherence and pseudonymisation — is a required starting point, but it does not clear a project of its broader socio-technical risks. The REC must apply a full ethical audit using the six evaluation parameters below.

panels.title: 1. Human Oversight — Will staff act automatically on AI alerts?

params.text: Will university support staff act automatically on these AI predictions, or will human professionals make the final intervention decision? What specific role does human judgement play in interpreting and validating the system's alerts? Is there a protocol ensuring humans remain 'in the loop'?

panels.title: 2. Bias & Fairness — Could the model reinforce inequalities?

params.text: The neural network is trained on 5 years of historical student data. If that history reflects existing social inequalities, the model may disproportionately flag students from lower-income backgrounds or minority groups as 'at-risk'. What concrete bias detection and mitigation strategies are in place? Has the model been tested across demographic subgroups?

panels.title: 3. Explainability — Can the prediction be explained?

params.text: When a student is labelled 'at-risk', both the student and the support staff need to understand exactly why. If the underlying neural network is a black box, the prediction cannot be adequately explained. This undermines both the student's right to understand decisions affecting them and the staff's ability to make informed interventions.

panels.title: 4. Privacy & Governance — Was secondary consent obtained for mental health data?

params.text: The proposal uses anonymised mental health service usage logs. Even pseudonymised, these are among the most sensitive categories of personal data. Did students explicitly consent to their mental health records being used for this AI system? Was this specific use covered by the original consent when students accessed mental health services?

panels.title: 5. Accountability — Who is responsible for misclassification?

params.text: If a student is incorrectly flagged as 'at-risk' and subsequently experiences academic stigma or unnecessary interventions, who assumes responsibility? The research team? The university? The algorithm developer? There must be a clear, documented accountability chain and an accessible redress mechanism for wrongly classified students.

panels.title: 6. Societal Impact — Could algorithmic labelling change how students are perceived?

params.text: Being algorithmically labelled 'at-risk' carries significant psychological and social weight. Could this tool inadvertently alter how teaching staff perceive and treat these students? Has the emotional and social impact of receiving an automated 'at-risk' designation been explicitly considered and addressed?

params.title: Smart Success — Key Concerns

dialogs.answer: The use of anonymised mental health service logs raises secondary consent issues — students may not have consented to this specific use of their sensitive data.
A model trained on historical data may disproportionately flag students from lower-income backgrounds if the training data reflects existing social inequalities.
If the neural network is a black box, the 'at-risk' prediction cannot be explained to the student or support staff.
If a student is misclassified and suffers academic stigma, who is responsible? The research proposal must define this clearly.

params.text:
The Proposal: Detecting Patient Deterioration with AI

A research team proposes deploying "Care4U" — an AI system designed to detect early signs of patient deterioration in a clinical hospital setting, with the goal of reducing unnecessary ICU admissions.

The system: Combines real-time biometric data streamed from wearable patient sensors with historical medical records. It continuously monitors vitals and sends automated alerts directly to ward nursing staff.

The model: A deep neural network trained on over 50,000 historical hospital cases.

Deployment: Live pilot study across two active hospitals.

Under the EU AI Act: Because it makes medical determinations affecting patient safety, this system likely qualifies as High-Risk AI, triggering strict regulatory requirements including a mandatory FRIA.

params.alt: Ethical Foresight in Clinical AI Innovation: The REC Review Checklist for Care4U — Human & Social Dimensions vs Technical & Legal Dimensions

metadata.title: Ethical Foresight in Clinical AI Innovation: The REC Review Checklist for Care4U — Human & Social Dimensions vs Technical & Legal Dimensions

params.text:
The REC Checklist: Two Dimensions

Deploying an algorithm in a live clinical environment means the stakes are life and death. The ethical scrutiny applied by the committee must scale to match that level of risk. The Care4U REC review checklist is organised into two complementary dimensions.

panels.title: Human & Social: Human Agency — Automation Bias

params.text: Will nurses rely too heavily on automated alerts, eroding their independent clinical judgement? As the system becomes embedded in routine ward operations, the risk of automation bias increases — nurses may begin to act on alerts without applying their own professional assessment. The proposal must specify protocols for maintaining independent human clinical judgement alongside the AI system.

panels.title: Human & Social: Bias & Fairness — Dataset Representation

params.text: The training dataset contains 50,000 historical hospital cases — a large number, but representativeness matters more than size. Could the system perform worse for women, older adults, or minority ethnic groups if those populations were underrepresented in the historical data? The proposal must provide demographic breakdowns of the training data and evidence of fairness testing.

panels.title: Human & Social: Societal Impact — Patient Anxiety & Doctor-Patient Relationship

params.text: Continuous algorithmic monitoring may significantly increase patient anxiety. The knowledge that a system is constantly assessing whether one is 'deteriorating' carries psychological weight. Additionally, could algorithmic alerts gradually shift the fundamental dynamic of the doctor-patient relationship — replacing clinical intuition with automated signals?

panels.title: Technical & Legal: Privacy & Consent — Opt-Out Without Penalty

params.text: Patients must be clearly informed about real-time data collection from wearable sensors. Critically, they must have the ability to opt out of the AI monitoring system without compromising their standard of care. If opting out means receiving lower-quality care, the consent cannot be considered truly free and voluntary.

panels.title: Technical & Legal: Explainability — The Black Box in Clinical Settings

params.text: Can clinicians actually understand why a specific alert was issued? If the system operates as a black box and clinicians cannot interpret the reasoning behind alerts, they face an impossible choice: blindly trust a machine or ignore the warning entirely. Neither is acceptable in a clinical setting. The proposal must specify what explainability mechanisms are built into the system.

panels.title: Technical & Legal: Accountability — When the System Fails

params.text: If the system misses a critical deterioration event, or issues a false alert that leads to the wrong treatment, who holds the legal and ethical responsibility? The research team? The hospital? The algorithm's developer? This must be unambiguously defined in the proposal, with documented redress pathways for affected patients.

params.title: Care4U — Key Concerns

dialogs.answer: Nurses may develop automation bias — over-relying on automated alerts and reducing their independent clinical judgement.
Patients must be able to opt out of AI monitoring without it compromising their standard of care.
If clinicians cannot understand why an alert was issued, they must choose between blindly trusting the machine or ignoring it — neither is safe.
If the system misses a deterioration event or triggers a false alert leading to wrong treatment, who is legally and ethically responsible?
As a medical AI making determinations about patient safety, Care4U likely qualifies as High-Risk AI — requiring conformity assessment and a mandatory FRIA.

Key Takeaways

You have completed Responsible Oversight in AI-Enabled Research. Here are the core insights to carry forward.

panels.title: The AI Lifecycle changes how we do ethics

params.text: AI research is not a static process. Ethics must be integrated across all four phases — Design, Development, Deployment, and Use & Monitoring. A single pre-approval review is insufficient for systems that adapt and evolve.

panels.title: Five questions underpin every AI ethics review

params.text: Every proposal must answer: What is the purpose? What data and methodology? How is consent ensured? How is data secured? What are the societal consequences — positive and negative?

panels.title: Ten principles define the ethical landscape of AI

params.text: Human Agency, Privacy, Transparency, Explainability, Fairness, Bias & Non-discrimination, Societal Well-being, Environmental Well-being, Accountability, and AI Convergence form an interconnected web of responsibilities. All must be addressed; none can be deferred.

panels.title: The EU AI Act makes ethics a legal obligation

params.text: The risk-based classification (Minimal → Unacceptable) determines what regulatory requirements apply. High-risk AI in sensitive sectors requires strict regulation and a mandatory FRIA before deployment.

panels.title: The right tool depends on the right context

params.text: ALTAI for early ethics-by-design, Ethics Canvas for participatory concept work, IEEE EAD for technical architects, Z-Inspection for high-stakes deployments, EU AI Act Compliance Checker for legal readiness. Choose based on audience, phase, and domain.

panels.title: Case studies show principles in practice

params.text: Smart Success (student dropout prediction) and Care4U (clinical patient monitoring) demonstrate that technical sophistication and legal compliance are necessary but not sufficient. Human oversight, explainability, and accountability must be built into the system — not treated as optional add-ons.

A Shared Responsibility

Maintaining rigorous ethical standards in AI research is not the exclusive domain of any single actor. It requires active, ongoing interdisciplinary collaboration between researchers, REC members, and policy makers. The novelty of a technological innovation can never serve as an excuse to bypass methodological scrutiny. Every time an AI-related proposal crosses your desk, apply the frameworks you have learned here — and ask the questions that protect the people behind the data.

Regulatory Frameworks

  • European Parliament and Council (2024). Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 — Artificial Intelligence Act. Official Journal of the European Union.
  • European Parliament and Council (2016). Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Official Journal of the European Union.

Ethics Guidelines & Assessment Tools

  • European Commission, High-Level Expert Group on AI (2019). Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI. European Commission.
  • European Commission (2020). Assessment List for Trustworthy AI (ALTAI) for Self-Assessment. European Commission.
  • IEEE (2019). Ethically Aligned Design: A Vision for Prioritizing Human Well-being with Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (1st ed.). IEEE.
  • UNESCO (2021). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. UNESCO.
  • OECD (2019). Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence. OECD.

Methodologies & Frameworks

  • Zicari, R. V. et al. (2021). Z-inspection: A Process to Assess Trustworthy AI. IEEE Transactions on Technology and Society, 2(2), 83–97.
  • Reijers, W. et al. (2018). Towards a Method for Ethical Analysis in the SHERPA Project. IEEE International Symposium on Ethics in Engineering, Science and Technology.
  • Floridi, L. et al. (2018). AI4People — An Ethical Framework for a Good AI Society. Minds and Machines, 28(4), 689–707.
  • The Turing Way Community (2022). The Turing Way: A Handbook for Reproducible, Ethical and Collaborative Research. Zenodo.
